name: Direct-to-consumer aligners (SmileDirectClub)
lead: Direct-to-consumer (DTC) aligners are clear plastic orthodontic aligners marketed straight to the public, usually through an online ordering process in which the patient takes dental impressions or scans at home or in a retail studio and a dentist or orthodontist reviews the case remotely. The best-known example was SmileDirectClub, a Nashville-based company founded in 2014 by Jordan Katzman and Alex Fenkell.[1]

The model was promoted as a lower-cost, more convenient alternative to braces and in-office aligners. Professional bodies, notably the American Association of Orthodontists, filed complaints with state dental boards about the company's practices, and a 2024 commentary in the Journal of the American Dental Association discussed the dilemma these products pose for patients and dentists.[1][5]

SmileDirectClub filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 29, 2023, and began liquidating in early 2024; its assets and technology were acquired by another Nashville company, SmileSet.[1] Other DTC aligner brands continue to exist.
infobox: Filed Chapter 11 in September 2023; liquidation effective January 2024

paras: Customers typically ordered an impression kit or visited a retail location, after which licensed dentists or orthodontists reviewed the records and oversaw treatment remotely. SmileDirectClub reportedly worked with about 225 licensed professionals and, despite its online model, operated around 300 retail locations across the United States, Canada, Australia and the United Kingdom.[1]

Survey research has examined why adults choose between an orthodontist, a general dentist and DTC aligners. A survey of 249 US adults looked at which patient factors influenced the choice of provider and the level of interest in each option, and a representative UK survey of 604 adults examined how perceived quality, cost, convenience, dental aesthetics, body image and mental health related to interest in orthodontic treatment.[2][4]

The company initially distributed aligners for Align Technology. A dispute over a non-compete clause led an arbitrator to order Align to close its retail locations and return its ownership stake, and in 2021 SmileDirectClub was ordered to pay Align $43.4 million plus interest.[1]

SmileDirectClub raised $380 million in October 2018 and expanded internationally. It listed on Nasdaq on September 12, 2019, at $23 per share, and closed its first day at $16.67.[1] After a failed sale, it announced in December 2023 that it would cease operations and move to Chapter 7 liquidation.[1]

The American Association of Orthodontists filed complaints with 36 state dental boards alleging regulatory violations. The company said 12 cases were closed with no adverse action, while the AAO said only five states had confirmed closures.[1]

A 2020 CBC Marketplace hidden-camera investigation reported that orthodontists who reviewed treatment plans approved by the company's network believed none should have been approved; the company disputed the findings and announced changes, including added staff training.[1] A 2019 false-advertising class action largely ended after most plaintiffs withdrew because consent forms required arbitration, and a 2020 lawsuit by the company against NBC News was dismissed in December 2021 under Tennessee's anti-SLAPP law.[1]
A study of the most popular YouTube patient testimonials compared braces, in-office aligners and DTC aligners, assessing their educational value and the sentiment of viewer comments.[3]
No studies found. Published research located on this topic consists of patient surveys, analyses of online video content and commentary rather than clinical trials of treatment outcomes.[2][3][4][5]

card.summary: Mail-order clear aligners that promised cheaper straight teeth; the flagship company went bankrupt in 2023 amid professional complaints.
card.note: Remote-supervised treatment drew complaints from orthodontist groups; SmileDirectClub ceased operations in 2023-24.

quick.overview:
Direct-to-consumer aligners are clear plastic trays ordered online after a home impression kit or a scan at a studio, with a dentist reviewing the case remotely. SmileDirectClub was the biggest name and pitched them as a cheaper, easier route to straighter teeth than braces.

The model drew complaints from orthodontic associations and dental boards, and the company filed for bankruptcy in 2023 and wound down in early 2024. Research located so far is mostly surveys and commentary rather than outcome trials.
quick.mechanism: Like other clear aligners, the trays are worn in sequence to move teeth gradually. The difference lies in the service model: the case is assessed from impressions or scans and monitored remotely rather than at in-person visits.
quick.risks: The American Association of Orthodontists filed complaints with state dental boards about the company, and a hidden-camera investigation reported that reviewing orthodontists disagreed with approved plans. The company disputed these characterizations. Published commentary in the dental literature describes the model as raising dilemmas for patients and clinicians.
